body.purpose: Every label, dropdown, and form text. macOS uses SF; Windows substitutes Segoe UI Variable at 14px; Linux substitutes Inter.

label.purpose: Form-group labels and result-list `dt` headings. Lighter via 70% opacity, not by hue.

value.purpose: The right column of the result list — the actual switch / port / VLAN strings the user came to read. Weight 500 differentiates them from labels at a glance.

status.purpose: The bottom-row status line. Carries 'Ready', 'Capturing LLDP packets…', 'Capture stopped', error messages.

footer.purpose: Quiet bookkeeping at the bottom — version string, locale picker label.

shadows.name: card-windows
shadows.purpose: Subtle Mica-style hint at the card edge on Windows light mode. Set to `none` in dark mode and on macOS / Linux.

shadows.name: card-macos-light
shadows.purpose: Almost-invisible hint that disambiguates the card edge from the vibrancy material behind it on macOS light. None in dark.

shadows.name: switch-thumb
shadows.purpose: The only meaningful shadow in the surface. Gives the iOS-style toggle thumb its physical-object feel.

motion.name: switch-state
motion.purpose: Toggle pill recolor and thumb slide. Both 200ms ease — short enough to feel responsive, long enough to read as movement.

motion.name: progress-loop
motion.purpose: Indeterminate capture progress. Fill slides from -100% to +300% of its container. Only animation in the system.

motion.name: reduced-motion-fallback
motion.purpose: When `prefers-reduced-motion` is set, the progress loop should be replaced with a non-animated indicator. Currently respected at the platform level via `prefers-reduced-motion` media query — explicit fallback styling is a follow-up.

breakpoints.name: fixed
breakpoints.purpose: PortFinder is a fixed-size desktop window. There is no responsive mobile layout — the window grows only when the privilege banner is present, via `setSize` from the Tauri window API.

components.name: Card (Controls / Result)
components.description: The two main sections of the app. Per-OS card chrome — values shown here are the macOS-light canonical.
components.css: .ds-card { background: #f7f7f7; border: 1px solid rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.05); border-radius: 10px; box-shadow: 0 1px 1px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.03); padding: 14px 18px; display: flex; flex-direction: column; gap: 13px; min-width: 280px; max-width: 360px; font-family: -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, 'SF Pro Text', sans-serif; font-size: 13px; line-height: 1.4; color: #1d1d1f; } .ds-card-row { display: grid; grid-template-columns: 70px 1fr; column-gap: 10px; align-items: baseline; } .ds-card-label { text-align: right; opacity: 0.7; font-size: 0.95em; } .ds-card-value { font-weight: 500; }

components.name: Switch (Off)
components.description: iOS-style toggle pill in the off state. Used for the 'Only show interfaces with an IP' control. Hand-built from a hidden checkbox.
components.css: .ds-switch-row { display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 48px; cursor: pointer; user-select: none; font-family: -apple-system, sans-serif; font-size: 0.92em; color: #1d1d1f; } .ds-switch-label { flex: 1; } .ds-switch-pill { position: relative; width: 40px; height: 18px; border-radius: 9px; background: rgba(29, 29, 31, 0.25); transition: background 0.2s ease; flex-shrink: 0; } .ds-switch-thumb { position: absolute; top: 2px; left: 2px; width: 22px; height: 14px; border-radius: 7px; background: #ffffff; box-shadow: 0 1px 2px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.25); transition: transform 0.2s ease; }

components.name: Switch (On)
components.description: Same component, on state. Track recolors to the system accent (shown as #007aff macOS blue here for the panel; in the live app it's `AccentColor` and follows the user's OS accent setting). Thumb translates 14px right.
components.css: .ds-switch-row { display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 48px; cursor: pointer; user-select: none; font-family: -apple-system, sans-serif; font-size: 0.92em; color: #1d1d1f; } .ds-switch-label { flex: 1; } .ds-switch-pill { position: relative; width: 40px; height: 18px; border-radius: 9px; background: #007aff; transition: background 0.2s ease; flex-shrink: 0; } .ds-switch-thumb { position: absolute; top: 2px; left: 2px; width: 22px; height: 14px; border-radius: 7px; background: #ffffff; box-shadow: 0 1px 2px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.25); transform: translateX(14px); transition: transform 0.2s ease; }

components.name: Progress Bar
components.description: Indeterminate capture indicator. Thin track with a fill that slides across, looping. The only animation in the system.
components.css: .ds-progress-bar { width: 100%; height: 3px; border-radius: 2px; background: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.12); overflow: hidden; } .ds-progress-fill { width: 35%; height: 100%; background: #007aff; border-radius: 2px; animation: ds-progress-slide 1.2s ease-in-out infinite; } @keyframes ds-progress-slide { 0% { transform: translateX(-100%); } 100% { transform: translateX(300%); } } @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { .ds-progress-fill { animation: none; width: 100%; opacity: 0.6; } }

components.name: Privilege Warning Banner
components.description: Sits above the Controls card when the app cannot capture (no BPF helper, no Npcap, no setcap). Uses Highlight / HighlightText system colors so it adopts whatever banner styling each OS prefers.
components.html: Packet capture requires BPF device access.
components.css: .ds-priv-warning { background: #cfe6ff; color: #0a4a82; border-radius: 6px; padding: 8px 12px; font-family: -apple-system, sans-serif; font-size: 0.92em; display: flex; flex-direction: column; gap: 6px; max-width: 340px; } .ds-priv-warning-msg { line-height: 1.4; } .ds-priv-warning-btn { align-self: flex-start; padding: 4px 12px; background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.6); color: inherit; border: 1px solid rgba(10, 74, 130, 0.25); border-radius: 4px; font: inherit; cursor: pointer; }

components.name: Locale Picker
components.description: Footer language picker. Native select with restrained chrome — transparent background, hairline border, low opacity, brightens on hover/focus.
components.css: .ds-locale-picker { background: transparent; border: 1px solid rgba(29, 29, 31, 0.25); border-radius: 4px; color: #1d1d1f; font-family: -apple-system, sans-serif; font-size: 0.78em; opacity: 0.7; padding: 1px 4px; cursor: pointer; transition: opacity 0.15s ease; } .ds-locale-picker:hover, .ds-locale-picker:focus-visible { opacity: 1; outline: none; }

narrative.overview:
PortFinder's in-app surface is, today, deliberately not a brand. It defers to whichever operating system you're running it under — the macOS build looks like Tahoe System Settings, the Windows build looks like Windows 11 Settings, the Linux build looks like a libadwaita boxed-list. Brand identity asserts itself at exactly one point: the dock icon. From the moment the window opens, the surface is whatever the OS provides — the system text color, the system accent color, the system focus ring, the platform's native widget rendering for `<select>`, `<button>`, `<input>`. The custom code is a thin layer of layout and chrome (cards, the iOS-style toggle, the capture progress bar) that sits on top of that native foundation.

This is a real design philosophy, not an unfinished one. The strategic case is that a small utility used in <30-second bursts under stress benefits from feeling like a built-in part of the machine — no cognitive cost of "what app's conventions are these," no mismatch between Settings-app focus styles and PortFinder focus styles. The trade-off is that PRODUCT.md's stated personality — *polished, branded, distinctive* — has nowhere to manifest in the current surface. The icon carries the entire identity load alone. Future iteration may move the surface in a more branded direction; this DESIGN.md captures what's actually rendered today, not what's wished for.
keyCharacteristics: System colors as the primary palette — no hex brand color appears in the rendered surface.
Per-OS font stack (SF, Segoe UI Variable, Inter) loaded by `data-os` attribute on `<html>`.
Per-OS card chrome: radius, padding, border, shadow all vary to match each platform's Settings-app idiom.
Light and dark via `color-scheme: light dark` plus `prefers-color-scheme` overrides per OS.
Two-card layout (Controls / Result) plus an optional Privilege Warning banner above.
One genuinely custom component: the iOS-style toggle switch, hand-built from `<input type="checkbox">` because no native checkbox renders the way the surrounding macOS surface needs.

rules.name: The System-First Rule
rules.body: Colors come from system CSS keywords (Canvas, CanvasText, AccentColor, Highlight, HighlightText, ButtonBorder) before they come from hex. If a value can be expressed as a system keyword, it is. Break it and the app starts feeling like a generic Electron utility instead of part of the OS.

rules.name: The Tint-Through-Function Rule
rules.body: Per-OS dividers and borders are computed from CanvasText via color-mix(in srgb, CanvasText X%, transparent), not hardcoded greys. Same in light mode, automatically inverts in dark mode, automatically respects per-OS subtlety differences.

rules.name: The No-Display-Tier Rule
rules.body: PortFinder's window is 400×460. There is no real estate for a 32px headline and there is no marketing voice that wants one. Type tops out at body weight; emphasis comes from weight contrast (500 vs 400) and opacity differentiation, not size.

rules.name: The Platform-Font Rule
rules.body: Body and value type both inherit from the per-OS family. Custom typeface choices are explicitly forbidden in the current system — picking 'Inter on every platform' would break Settings-on-Every-Machine for the marginal gain of consistency.

rules.name: The Tonal-Layer Rule
rules.body: Card depth = page-color one step + a hairline border. Don't reach for box-shadow to communicate 'this is a card' — that's what the Bootstrap-shadow-on-everything aesthetic does, and it's the generic Electron trap.

dos: Do rely on system colors first. Canvas, CanvasText, AccentColor, Highlight, HighlightText, ButtonBorder carry the bulk of the surface. If a value can be expressed as one, express it that way.
Do respect the user's system accent color. Don't hardcode blue. AccentColor is the contract.
Do vary per-OS chrome via html[data-os="..."] — radius, padding, font stack, surface color all change deliberately. The variation is the point.
Do use color-mix(in srgb, CanvasText X%, transparent) for borders, dividers, and tints. This auto-inverts in dark mode and respects per-OS subtlety.

Do carry state via text and icon, not color alone. Capture state ('Ready' / 'Capturing LLDP packets…' / 'Capture stopped') is a textual status, not a colored dot. Error state is a red status text and the word 'Error' — not red text alone. Color-blind safety is a hard constraint, not a polish item.
Do keep type one tier deep. There is no Display, no Headline. Body and label, weight contrast and opacity contrast carry hierarchy.

Do keep motion to one place. The capture progress bar is the only animation in the system. Add more only when motion makes a state change clearer, never decoratively. Respect prefers-reduced-motion as a calm fallback.
donts: Don't ship a generic Electron aesthetic. PRODUCT.md names this directly: same Bootstrap-ish components as fifty other utilities, every widget rounded the same way, no rooting in any visual tradition. The current design exists in opposition to that — preserve the 'this looks like Settings' reading, don't drift into 'looks like a cross-platform tool that picked a Material theme.'
Don't add decorative gradients, gradient text, or background-clip: text. PRODUCT.md rejects flashy SaaS-dashboard chrome by name.
Don't add side-stripe borders (border-left: 4px solid color) on the privilege warning, the result rows, or anything else. Use full borders, background tints, leading icons, or nothing.
Don't add a hero metric / hero number. There's no marketing surface inside the app.

Don't glassmorphism the cards. The macOS vibrancy is a system feature delivered by NSVisualEffectView, applied once at the window level — that's the only 'glass' in the system. Don't paint additional backdrop-filter: blur() on cards, banners, or the locale picker.

Don't override native widget chrome with custom CSS. button, select, input keep their platform appearance. The toggle switch is the only exception, and it's hand-built specifically to read correctly inside an opaque card.

Don't introduce a brand color into the surface unless the design direction explicitly changes. Today the brand color (icon navy / amber) lives only in the icon. Adding it to a button or accent in the app would break Settings-on-Every-Machine without replacing it with an articulated alternative.
Don't use modals. The privilege warning is a banner, not a dialog. Inline > modal in this app.
Don't stack the Controls and Result cards with extra padding between them. The 8px gap on .app is the single source of vertical rhythm — adding margin-top on a card breaks it.
Don't introduce em dashes in copy. Commas, colons, periods, parentheses do the work.
